assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ripple
items.clue: A wave on a water surface.

items.label: Period
items.clue: The time for one complete wave to pass a point.

items.label: Hertz
items.clue: The unit meaning one complete wave each second.

items.label: Oscillation
items.clue: The repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down movement of a particle of the medium about a fixed position as a wave passes.

questions.stem: A student uses [v = f λ] with the frequency in hertz and the wavelength in metres. What unit does the calculated wave speed have?

options.text: Hertz, Hz, the unit taken from the frequency
Metres, m, the unit taken from the wavelength
Seconds, s, because speed always involves a time
Metres per second, m/s, since the answer is a speed

questions.explanation: The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s.

questions.stem: A sound wave has a frequency of 2.5 kHz. What is this frequency in hertz?

options.text: 250 Hz
25 Hz

questions.stem: Ripples on a tank have a wavelength of 40 cm and a frequency of 5 Hz. What is their wave speed?

options.text: 2 m/s
2 m

questions.stem: A wave is shown on a graph of displacement against distance. How are the amplitude and the wavelength read from it?

options.text: Amplitude runs from a trough up to the crest above it
Both are measured along the horizontal distance axis
Amplitude is vertical, wavelength is horizontal
Wavelength runs from one crest to the next trough

questions.explanation: Amplitude is read up the displacement axis, wavelength along the distance axis.

questions.stem: A class measures the speed of sound in air. Which method gives the most reliable value?

options.text: Time the echo of a clap from a wall a measured distance away
Measure how loud the clap is at two different distances
Use a stopwatch to time a clap crossing the laboratory
Ask two students to clap together and time the delay

questions.explanation: A long path gives a time large enough for reaction time to matter little; speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time.

questions.stem: In the echo method for the speed of sound, the distance to the wall is measured but twice that distance is used in the calculation. Why?

options.text: Because the sound must spread out in every direction from the clap
Because the wall creates a new wave that travels more slowly
Because the sound travels to the wall and back before it is heard
Because sound travels faster on its way back from the wall

questions.explanation: The timed interval covers two equal journeys, so the path is 2 × the distance to the wall.

questions.stem: Which is a suitable method for measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface?

options.text: Count the ripples reaching the far edge and multiply by the depth
Use the dipper frequency and a measured wavelength in v = f λ
Measure the height of the ripples and divide it by the frequency
Time one ripple with a stopwatch over a two centimetre gap

questions.explanation: Frequency is read from the signal generator and wavelength from the projected pattern.

questions.stem: Why is a stroboscope or a video recording often used when ripples are studied in a ripple tank?

options.text: It increases the frequency of the ripples on the water surface
A stopwatch would time the ripples just as well
It makes the ripples taller so the amplitude can be measured
It freezes the pattern so wavelengths can be measured

questions.explanation: A still pattern lets a ruler be laid across ten wavelengths on the projected image.

questions.stem: (Physics only) A sound wave passes from air into water, where it travels faster. What happens to its frequency and its wavelength?

options.text: The wavelength stays the same and the frequency increases
Both the frequency and the wavelength become larger
The frequency stays the same and the wavelength becomes longer
The frequency stays the same and the wavelength gets shorter

questions.explanation: With f fixed and v larger, v = f λ requires λ to increase in the same proportion.

questions.stem: (Physics only) Sound travels faster in a steel rail than in air. When a sound passes from the air into the steel, which quantity is fixed by the source and cannot change?

options.text: The frequency, which is set by the vibrating source
The wave speed, which depends on the source's energy
The wavelength, because the wave keeps its shape
The period, which grows longer in the steel

questions.explanation: The source sends the same number of waves each second whatever medium receives them.

questions.stem: In required practical activity 8, which apparatus is most suitable for measuring the wavelength of ripples in a ripple tank?

options.text: A ruler measuring across just one ripple
A ruler measuring the height of a single ripple crest
A stopwatch timing one ripple crossing the tank
A ruler placed under the projected ripple pattern

questions.explanation: The projected pattern is still enough to measure across, ideally over ten wavelengths.

questions.stem: In required practical activity 8, waves are also sent along a stretched string. Why is the distance across ten wavelengths measured and then divided by ten?

options.text: The wavelength changes as the wave crosses the whole string
It reduces the effect of uncertainty in each reading
Measuring one wavelength alone would give the same result
Ten readings must be taken in every school experiment

questions.explanation: The same ruler uncertainty is a much smaller fraction of a ten-times-longer distance.

questions.stem: Which unit does the specification give for momentum, p?

options.text: kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
kilogram per metre second, kg/m s
newtons per second squared, N/s²
newton metres per second, N m/s

questions.explanation: The unit printed in 4.5.7.1, and the one built by multiplying kg by m/s.

questions.stem: Two skaters stand at rest on ice and push each other apart. Which statement about their momentum is correct?

options.text: They have equal and opposite momenta, so the total is still zero, as it was before the push
Both of the skaters are now moving, so the system has gained momentum from the push they gave
Each skater simply keeps the momentum it began with, which was zero for both
Their momenta add together, giving twice the momentum that one skater has on its own

questions.stem: (physics only) In the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what does the quantity m ∆ v represent?

options.text: The force acting on the object, because force equals the change in momentum
The change in momentum, that is the mass multiplied by the change in velocity
The total momentum the object had before the force began to act on it, in kg m/s
The change in the force acting, which is the mass multiplied by the change in acceleration

questions.explanation: The specification states directly that m ∆ v = change in momentum.

questions.stem: A ball has a mass of 400 g and travels at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?

options.text: 2 kg m/s
80 kg m/s
0.4 kg m/s
2000 kg m/s

questions.stem: (physics only) A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg trolley. They stick together. What is their velocity after the collision?

options.text: 4 m/s
12 kg m/s

questions.explanation: Momentum before = 3 × 4 = 12 kg m/s. Afterwards the moving mass is 5 kg, so v = 12 / 5 = 2.4 m/s.

questions.stem: (physics only) The specification says force equals the rate of change of momentum. What does 'rate of' add?

options.text: Nothing of substance; the force is simply equal to the change in momentum that takes place
That the momentum is multiplied by the time for which the resultant force acts on the object
That the change in momentum is divided by the time taken for that change to happen
That the momentum changes at a steady rate whenever any resultant force acts on an object
